heading: Summary
content: This document presents LNA namely the Site Safety and Resource Management System tailord for pipeline locations. The solution is mobile-based which provides ease of transferability and deployment at any locations. LNA AIplatform brings the power of advanced analytics and machine learning to the on-premise edge environment enabling a new class of applications for advanced monitoring and diagnostics, machine performance optimization, proactive maintenance and operational intelligence use cases.

heading: Objective
content: The objective of the solutions is to enhance the worker safety environment at operational sites by deploying AI-enabled solutions. With mobile infrastructure it provides reusable hardware to reduce ROI, the system utilizes CCTV camera streams and BLE smart tags technology in performing real-time video stream analytics and RTLS to monitor and enhance worker safety environment. By adopting a reliable, practical and intelligent systems, it can save operational cost associated with manual enforcement of safety regulations and above all can save and maintain worker health and safety conditions.

heading: Scope and Considerations
content:
Saudi Aramco is currently reviewing the implementation of an AI-based Video Analytics System to enhance HSE monitoring and incident prevention for the Fadhili Gas Increment Project, PKG2, which is an Aramco construction project in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The system is intended to strengthen site worker safety, support real-time hazard detection, and enable proactive incident prevention across all monitored work locations.

The solution is an AI-driven video analytics platform that integrates with the existing CCTV infrastructure to monitor construction site locations, enforce HSE compliance through automated detection of hazards, and relay actionable alerts back to the CCTV Control Rooms to mitigate incidents. The site will be equipped with the following:

AI-enabled CCTV analytics for site safety monitoring, with the following detection features:

  1. Safety Helmet (Hard Hat) Detection

  2. Full PPE Compliance Detection (vest, footwear, gloves, eye and face protection)

  3. Fire and Smoke Detection

  4. Fall Detection

  5. Restricted Area Intrusion Detection

  6. Confined Space Entry Monitoring

  7. Working at Height Violation Detection

  8. Excavation Safety Monitoring

  9. Lifting and Rigging Operations Monitoring

  10. Vehicle and Driving Safety Monitoring

  11. Heavy Equipment Safety Monitoring

  12. Trip Hazard Detection

  13. Fire Detection

  14. Hot Work Monitoring

  15. Smoking in Prohibited Areas

  16. Barricade and Safety Control Tampering

The existing cameras specs are only 2 MP whereas we always perfer 5 MP or higher as per Aramco standard for the system to achieve highest possible accuracy for the detection. 

Integration with existing CCTV infrastructure, comprising approximately 22 CCTV units currently in operation:

  1. 5 Fixed Cameras (PTZ Type)

  2. 7 Trailer-Mounted CCTV Systems (PTZ Type)

  3. 10 Mobile Cameras (Fixed Type)

  • Real-time monitoring from the two (2) existing dedicated CCTV Control Rooms.

  • Visual and audible alarms generated automatically during detection events for immediate operator response.

  • Independent operation utilizing existing CCTV video streams, without requiring replacement of current camera hardware.

  • Configurable AI functions, allowing individual detection modules to be enabled or disabled independently per location or operational requirement.

  • Continuous performance improvement capability to progressively reduce false positives and false negatives over time.

  • Resilient operation under desert environmental conditions, including high temperature, dust, sand, and strong winds, while accommodating limited telecommunications and network infrastructure on site.

  • Operation and maintenance support, provided on the basis that no dedicated AI specialist is available on site, ensuring practical day-to-day usability by existing personnel.

  • Scalable architecture supporting future expansion in cameras, locations, and detection functions without major hardware or software replacement.

heading: LNA Site Resource Management Solution
content:
LNA Site Resource Management System uses active technology to monitor workers, vehicals and assets it works on latest version of BLE gateways, anchor beacons and the Long-Range gps enabled active tags which constantly advertise their information in an active mode, the chargeable batteries are long lasting . The gateways convey information to the servers which analize the information and provide accurate location, head counts and information related to the individual tag on the Dash Board to the user.

Key Elements of Site Resource Managment :

  • Personal Tracking Devices: These devices ensure worker safety in work area

environments by providing real-time location tracking and emergency SOS

functionalities.

  • Smartwatches: Used by supervisors and field operators, these devices support

geofencing, zone management, and emergency alerts, ensuring seamless

communication and operational oversight.

  • On-Cloud Software Platform: The system includes a dedicated software

platform installed on a secure server in the control room, managing all tracking data, alerts, and system configurations.

  • BLE Network Infrastructure: The backbone of the tracking solution, this

infrastructure includes gateways with GPS and cellular communications to ensure

reliable communication across the plant.

BLE Gateways

The selected IoT gateway is a high-performance Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE 5.x) gateway designed to ensure reliable, extended-range communication for IoT applications. This gateway is ideal for large-scale deployments and provides robust connectivity across the expansive and challenging terrain of the construction site. Below is a detailed technical description of its key features.

High Capacity and Coverage:

  • High-Density Device Handling: Operating in continuous scanning mode across the three BLE primary advertising channels (37, 38, 39), the gateway captures broadcast packets from hundreds of worker tags simultaneously without requiring a paired connection to each device. It additionally supports up to 16 concurrent GATT connections for configuration, diagnostics, and firmware updates on individual devices. This is crucial for handling the large number of worker devices deployed on site.

  • Extended-Range Communication: Support for the BLE 5.x LE Coded PHY (Long Range) extends effective coverage well beyond classic BLE, achieving several hundred metres line-of-sight, so data from worker devices is transmitted reliably across open construction areas. Gateways are deployed in an overlapping grid to eliminate coverage gaps around structures, plant, and material stockpiles.

  • Flexible Backhaul: Captured data is forwarded to the network server over Ethernet/PoE, Wi-Fi, or 4G/LTE using MQTT or HTTPS, allowing gateways to be sited according to coverage requirements rather than cabling constraints.

  • Environmental Suitability: IP-rated enclosures with wide operating-temperature tolerance and PoE power delivery suit outdoor, dust-exposed installation on temporary site infrastructure.

BLE Network Server

  • High-Capacity Device Management: The BLE Network Server manages, authenticates, and maintains the registry of all end devices, capable of handling thousands of tags and beacons concurrently. This makes it ideal for expansive IoT deployments.

  • Data Handling and Routing: Efficiently processes and routes advertisement and telemetry packets from end devices to application servers. Because a single tag is typically heard by several gateways at once, the server performs cross-gateway deduplication while retaining the per-gateway RSSI values needed for proximity, zoning, and trilateration. Advertising intervals and transmit power are tuned per device profile to balance location accuracy, airtime, and battery life.

  • Enhanced Security: Maintains data integrity and confidentiality through BLE LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256 pairing) with AES-128-CCM link-layer encryption, Resolvable Private Addresses to prevent tag tracking by third parties, and TLS-secured MQTT/HTTPS on the gateway backhaul. Device identity and key material are centrally provisioned and revocable.

  • Network Performance and Gateway Management: Actively monitors gateway health, uptime, scan throughput, and packet-loss rates, and manages remote configuration and firmware updates across the gateway fleet to ensure comprehensive coverage and reliability. Tag battery levels and last-seen timestamps are tracked to flag devices requiring service.

  • Application Integration: Offers robust REST API, MQTT, and webhook support for seamless integration with user applications, facilitating data access, device management, real-time location streaming, and network monitoring.

  • Scalability and Customization: The platform is highly scalable, suitable for both small and large-scale IoT networks, and can be customized to meet specific operational requirements including zone definitions, geofence rules, and alert thresholds particular to the site.

heading: LNL-X2220
content: The LNL-X2220 Intelligent Dual Reader Controller (IDRC) by Lenel provides a single board solution for interfacing one or two doors to an OnGuard system. In addition, other I/O and reader interface modules can be added on the LNL-X2220’s downstream port to expand its capabilities. The LNL-X2220 revolutionizes access control system architecture by allowing Ethernet connection directly from an entry location to the OnGuard server, while still providing the security, functionality, and modularity of LENEL’s proven hardware platform. The LNL-X2220 is scalable for any access control application, from the most basic to the most sophisticated. In the event of communication loss, the LNL-X2220 allows nearly all local functionality to continue unimpaired until the server connection is restored. Utilizing its native Ethernet communications and an advanced 32- bit processor, the LNL-X2220 can communicate upstream to the host computer through its Ethernet port (with a throughput up to eight times greater than the fastest serial connections), or at up to 115.2 Kbps using RS-232 communication directly or through an external dial-up modem. The LNL-X2220 can store up to 250,000 cardholders in non- volatile flash memory and supports selective download for larger cardholder databases. The downstream RS-485 two-wire port can be used to connect up to 32 devices (maximum 64 doors). Two on-board reader ports support Data1/Data0, Clock/Data, Bios crypt RS-485 readers and the bidirectional RS-485 Open Supervised Device Protocol (OSDP) communications. Each LNL-X2220 supports up to eight different card formats. The LNL X2220 includes eight inputs that support normally open, normally closed, supervised, and unsupervised circuits. In addition, four output relays support fail-safe or fail-secure operation.

heading: LNL-1320-S3
content: Lenel offers a Dual Reader Interface (DRI) module for access control solutions. Most access control card readers, keypads, or readers with keypads that use standard Wiegand Data1/Data0 or Clock/Data communication are supported, as are those that support the bidirectional RS-485 Open Supervised Device Protocol (OSDP). Lock, unlock, and facility code offline access modes are supported on all readers connected to the DRI. Each DRI supports up to eight different card formats as well as issue codes for both magnetic and Wiegand card formats. The DRI provides a vital link between the Intelligent System Controller (ISC) and the card reader attached to the interface. As many as 32 DRI modules can be multidrop using RS-485 2-wire or 4-wire communication up to 4,000 feet per port away from the ISC. Each DRI module is individually addressed for increased reporting capabilities with OnGuard® access control software applications. The DRI includes eight inputs that support normally open, normally closed, supervised, and non-supervised circuits. In addition, six output relays support fail-safe or fail-secure operation.

heading: Crash Rated Barriers (Road Blockers)
content: The Gates shall be equipped with ASTM M50-P1 as defined in ASTM F2656-07 or PAS 68 or ISO/IWA 14-1 (as long as they are rated equivalent to the ASTM rating of M50-P1) crash-rated Hydraulic Raise Barriers or Rising Kerb Road Blockers, to ensure that no large vehicle can break through. These barriers shall be certified to PAS68 or U.S Department of State test standard SD-STD-2.01 Revision A. Barriers shall also comply with SAIS Directives SEC-03 and SEC-06. Crash Rated Barriers shall be supplied complete with all safety loops, and two color traffic lights to provide visual verification that it is safe to pass. The crash barrier shall be constructed of steel that complies with either ASTM 514 or ASTM 517 standards and shall fully comply with SAIS SEC-06 / 5.3.3.

heading: Static Bollards
content: The crash-rated static bollards shall be deployed to ensure containment at the entrance gates as illustrated in the Main Gate drawings. The crash rating of these static bollards shall match that of the associated barrier. These bollards shall be certified to ASTM F2656-07 M50 P1 or its equivalent in BS PAS-68 or its equivalent in ISO/IWA 14-1 standard.

heading: Raise Arm Barriers
content: The Main Gate shall be controlled by raising arm barriers, which shall be interlocked with road blockers and interfaced with the EACS via the ISS. These systems will be deployed at both entry and exit points. All raising arm barriers and accessories shall comply with SEC-05 and SEC-06 standards. These barriers shall be high-speed units, with a maximum 6-second cycle time. Each entrance shall be equipped with an ACS Proximity & PIN reader for entry. Exit shall be via ACS Proximity & PIN reader, to allow the ACS system to maintain an accurate muster role. All drop gates shall be constructed of materials and components that will permit extended, continuous operation under the environmental conditions specified in SEC-01 and shall be compliant with SAIS SEC-06 / 5.3.1.

heading: Crash Rated Manual Raise Arm Barriers
content:
4.1 General Overview

The vehicle entry and exit lanes shall be protected by high-security, heavy-duty drop arm crash beam barriers (A-1 Alcazar CBB or approved equal). The system shall provide physical hostile vehicle mitigation (HVM) at main gate access points, fully integrated with the site Enterprise Access Control System (EACS) and Integrated Security System (ISS) management platform.

4.2 Standard & Regulatory Compliance

  • Crash Performance Certification: The barrier assembly shall be physically crash-tested and certified to ASTM F2656-07 M50-P1 standards (capable of stopping a 6,800 kg / 15,000 lb medium-duty truck traveling at 80 km/h / 50 mph with dynamic penetration  ≤ 1.0 m). Equivalent compliance with PAS 68 or ISO/IWA 14-1 at the M50-P1 energy rating is acceptable.

  • Directive Compliance: Fully compliant with SAIS Directives SEC-01 (Environmental Limits), SEC-03 (Perimeter Barriers), SEC-05 (Access Control Points), and SEC-06 / 5.3.3 & 5.3.1 (Vehicle Access Control Equipment & Drop Gates).

4.3 Mechanical Construction & Finish

  • Beam & Stanchion Construction: The crash beam and main pivot/locking stanchions shall be constructed from high-yield structural steel meeting ASTM A514 or ASTM A517 standards.

  • Protective Coating: Structural elements shall be hot-dip galvanized per ASTM A123 / BS EN ISO 1461 and finished with an architectural-grade, high-durability polyester powder coating or thermoplastic finish, UV-stabilized for extreme desert ambient conditions (0 ∘C to  + 55 ∘C, direct sunlight, high humidity, and sandstorm environments).

  • Clear Span: Designed to cover clear driveway openings up to 6.0 meters (20 ft) per lane.

4.4 Drive System & Performance

  • Cycle Time: High-speed hydraulic drive mechanism providing full opening and closing stroke within  ≤ 6 seconds, satisfying high-throughput peak shift requirements.

  • Drive Mechanism: Industrial-grade hydraulic power unit (HPU) housed within a heavy-gauge, weather-sealed NEMA 4X / IP66 enclosure.

  • Manual Override: Equipped with a manual hydraulic hand pump and mechanical release to enable manual raising/lowering during total power failure.

heading: Intrusion Detection and Assessment System (IDAS)
content:
The purpose of the PIDS is to protect against intrusion threats. The objective of the perimeter intrusion detection system (PIDS) is to detect any intrusion or intrusion attempt. Sensors have been distributed along a main perimeter. A measure of how closely the system can identify the specific location where the intrusion attempt was detected, main perimeters is divided into alarm zones. According to 2017 SAIS directives, main perimeters are divided into 150 meters, but in some cases due to site outer limit constraints the zone can be less or slightly greater than that value. Alarm zone distribution is to have a good probability of detection, with low rate of nuisance and false alarm.

The IDAS is comprised of two types of field sensors and fixed CCTV cameras:

  1. MIDS which detects movement inside the microwave barrier range.

    FSS (FENCE SENSOR SYSTEM) which detects vibration, cutting & lifting on a Chain link fence.

heading: Fence Sensor System (FSS)
content:
FSS shall be installed in center of Anti-Personnel Fence Fabric, and along the Concertina.

FSS must detect an intruder climbing (slow and fast), jumping, cutting (slow and fast), breaking in the fence in no more than one minute by any means of penetration through the fence fabric with the specified Probability of Detection (PD) and Confidence Factor (CF).

There shall not be any “dead zones” on the fence inclusive of culverts or other unique fence crossings.

FSS shall employ point impact discrimination which detects single location activity while rejecting other distributed environmental conditions (wind, rain, or other environmental disturbances). The Alarm Processing Unit shall utilize both temporal and spatial filtering.

The perimeter fence has been divided into physical zones, with a maximum length of 150 meters per zone.

heading: MIDS
content:
Microwave Intrusion Detection System (MIDS) develops a volumetric electromagnetic beam between the transmitter and the receiver, using high frequency microwaves, and creating an invisible but sensitive detection wall. Perturbation of the beam generates an alarm. The system is adapted to various site conditions or changes in weather patterns. A specific attention is paid during microwave sensor selection to comply with SAIS temperature and humidity standards for outdoor equipment (SAIS DIR SEC 01§ 4.2.3). The microwave units detect at minimum of 35 kg human - walking, running, hands and knees crawling, jumping, rolling or prone crawling (30.5 cm diameter metal sphere) at a target velocity of 30 mm/sec to 15 m/sec. The microwave units have field adjustable sensitivity control. The microwave system provides an internal and external alignment, sensitivity adjustment, and input power indication that may be displayed and monitored.

The Maximum typical distance between MIDS transmitter (Tx) and receiver (Rx) are 183 meters (i.e., 150m zone and 10m overlap to cover the dead zone under each head) Or depending upon on the terrain of the perimeter. They are mounted on hot deep galvanized, 1-meter height pole. The microwave barriers will be powered locally through POE from the IES within the nearest FEC.

The Model 334 operates at K-band frequency (24.125 GHz), offering performance advantages over traditional X-band microwave links (10.5 GHz). Its antenna beam width is approximately 11 degrees in both horizontal and vertical planes, enabling effective operation over long ranges and within defined corridors.

Each Model 334 Transmitter and Receiver is housed in a weatherproof enclosure, measuring 269 mm (10.6 in) in diameter and weighing 2.0 kg (4.5 lbs). In contrast, comparable X-band systems often require larger housings of 609 mm (24 in) in diameter and weigh around 15.9 kg (35 lbs). The compact size of the Model 334 provides optimal resistance to wind-loading and offers clear advantages for installation and shipping.

Operating at a frequency 2.5 times higher than X-band, the Model 334 generates a multipath signal that is also 2.5 times higher, enhancing the detection of slow-moving intruders. Its precise beam control and higher multipath frequency contribute to superior detection performance.

The receiver's advanced design increases detection probability by alarming on partial or complete beam interruption, signal level fluctuations, or jamming attempts by other transmitters. An Automatic Gain Control (AGC) circuit allows the receiver to adapt to varying site conditions and weather changes.

Operating in the less crowded K-band spectrum, the Model 334 is inherently less susceptible to external interference from airport landing systems, aircraft or marine radar, and other microwave intrusion systems. It features six crystal-controlled, field-selectable modulation channels with narrow-band filtering, allowing multiple Model 334 units to operate together without mutual interference. Additionally, units can be dual, triple, or quad-stacked with Model 336 K-Band Digital Microwave Links to enhance security in applications with risks of prone crawling or bridging attacks.

The microwave system is designed to support detection zones of up to 183 meters (600 feet).

6. SECURITY CONTROL EQUIPMENT-

Video Management System (VMS) A Video Management System (VMS) is software designed to manage, record, and monitor video streams from multiple surveillance cameras in a security setup. It allows users to view live or recorded video, control cameras (e.g., pan, tilt, zoom), and configure settings for video storage, retrieval, and analysis. VMS integrates with other security components, such as access control systems and alarm systems, providing a centralized platform for surveillance and security management across various locations.

Genetec Security Center (5.12)

Security Center is a unified security platform. It incorporates access control, video surveillance, automatic license plate recognition (ALPR), communications, and more into a single, intuitive solution. With a platform that unifies your data, you can manage security policies, run investigations, and pay attention to what matters most. Turn on new capabilities when you need them and choose the devices and add-ons that make sense for you as your system grows.

heading: Network Video Recording (NVR)
content: A Network Video Recorder (NVR) is a specialized device used in IP-based surveillance systems to record, store, and manage video footage from network cameras. Unlike traditional DVRs, which work with analog cameras, NVRs are designed to process digital video streams directly over a network. They typically offer features like remote access, live viewing, playback, and storage management, and can be integrated with video management systems (VMS) to provide a comprehensive video surveillance solution.

  • VMS FAILOVER

VMS FAILOVER: Failover is a backup operational mode in which a role (system function) is automatically transferred from its primary server to a secondary server that is on standby. This transfer between servers occurs only if the primary server becomes unavailable, either through failure or through scheduled downtime. Role failover is managed by the Directory role.

How role failover works in Security Center For failover to work in Security Center, you need to define the following two types of servers: Primary Server: Server that normally hosts a role for it to work on the system.

Secondary Server: Servers on standby that are assigned to a role to keep it running in case the primary server becomes unavailable.

There is no limit to the number of secondary (or standby) servers you can assign to most roles. However, the more servers you add, the less cost-effective it might be for you. The secondary server of one role can be the primary server of another role, provided that both servers have enough resources (CPU, memory, disk space, and network bandwidth) to handle the combined load of both roles in case of a failover.

IMPORTANT: Security Center does not handle the failover of role databases. For roles that connect to a database, the database server will be hosted on a third computer, separate from the servers hosting the role. All role servers will have read and write access to the database server. To protect your data, perform regular backups of the role database. Before failover, a role is hosted on the primary server and connects to a database server hosted on a third computer. When the primary server fails, the role automatically fails over to the secondary server and reconnects to the same database

heading: PAGA System in a Plant
content:
PAGA stands for Public Address and General Alarm. It is a critical communication and emergency notification system used in industrial plants, oil & gas facilities, petrochemical plants, power plants, refineries, and other hazardous environments.

The main purpose of a PAGA system is to broadcast voice announcements and emergency alarms throughout the plant so that personnel can receive clear instructions during normal operation, emergencies, evacuation, fire, gas release, or other hazardous conditions.

Main Functions

  1. Public Address (PA)

    • Routine operational announcements.

    • Paging between control rooms, field areas and personnel.

    • Broadcast of maintenance or safety instructions.

    • Live announcements from operator stations.

  2. General Alarm (GA)

    • Fire alarm notification.

    • Gas release alarm.

    • Emergency evacuation alarm.

    • Plant shutdown or emergency instructions.

    • Pre-recorded emergency messages.

  3. Emergency Communication

    • Allows operators to communicate with personnel in affected areas.

    • Provides zone-based or plant-wide announcements.

    • Can prioritize emergency messages over normal paging.

Typical PAGA System Architecture

A typical system consists of:

Control Room → PAGA Controller/Server → Network → Amplifiers → Speakers

Major equipment includes:

Equipment Function
PAGA Controller / Server Central system control and configuration
Operator Console Live paging and alarm initiation
Microphone Station Voice announcements
Power Amplifier Amplifies audio signals
Horn / Trumpet Speaker Outdoor/industrial sound coverage
Ceiling / Wall Speaker Indoor sound coverage
Explosion-Proof Speaker Hazardous-area applications
Beacon / Strobe Visual alarm indication
Call Station / Intercom Station Two-way communication where required
Network Switch IP communication between system devices
Amplifier Monitoring Detects amplifier/speaker-line faults
UPS Backup power for critical equipment

PAGA in Hazardous Areas

For an oil & gas or petrochemical plant, equipment installed in hazardous areas must be appropriately certified, such as ATEX/IECEx, depending on the project requirements and hazardous-area classification.

Typical field devices may include:

  • Explosion-proof speakers

  • Weatherproof speakers

  • Explosion-proof call stations

  • Weatherproof paging stations

  • Visual alarm beacons

  • Certified junction boxes

PAGA vs. Normal PA System

Feature Normal PA PAGA
Routine announcements ✓ ✓
Emergency alarms Limited ✓
Evacuation messages Limited ✓
Fire & gas interface Usually no ✓
Zone-based alarm Sometimes ✓
Speaker-line supervision Usually no ✓
Amplifier redundancy Optional Typically required
Hazardous-area equipment Optional Often required
Emergency priority Limited ✓
Industrial plant application Limited Designed for this

Example of Plant Operation

If a gas leak is detected by the Fire & Gas System:

Gas Detector → Fire & Gas System → PAGA System → Emergency Alarm → Speakers/Strobes → Personnel

The PAGA system can automatically broadcast a predefined message such as:

"Attention. Gas release has been detected in Area 3. Evacuate the area immediately and proceed to the designated muster point."

The system can also activate the appropriate alarm tone and visual indicators.

Important PAGA Design Features

For an industrial plant, the PAGA system should normally be designed with:

  • High availability

  • Amplifier redundancy

  • Speaker-line supervision

  • Fault monitoring

  • Emergency priority

  • Zone selection

  • Fire & Gas System interface

  • UPS-backed power

  • Network redundancy where applicable

  • Hazardous-area certified field equipment

  • Continuous system diagnostics

  • Fail-safe operation

In a plant, PAGA is therefore more than a normal loudspeaker system—it is a critical life-safety and emergency communication system used to alert and direct personnel throughout the facility.

heading: Plant Alert System
content:
A Plant Alert System is an industrial notification system used to inform personnel about abnormal, hazardous, or emergency conditions within a plant. It provides rapid visual, audible, and/or voice-based warnings so that personnel can take the required safety action.

In an industrial facility such as an oil & gas plant, refinery, petrochemical facility, gas plant, or power plant, the Plant Alert System is normally integrated with systems such as Fire & Gas (F&G), Emergency Shutdown (ESD), PAGA, SCADA/DCS, and other plant monitoring systems.

Main Purpose

The system is designed to:

  • Alert personnel when an abnormal condition occurs.

  • Provide area-specific or plant-wide warnings.

  • Generate audible and visual alarms.

  • Display the affected area or alarm condition.

  • Provide predefined emergency messages where required.

  • Interface with the Fire & Gas and control systems.

  • Support evacuation and emergency response.

  • Maintain alarm history and event records.

Typical Plant Alert Architecture

A typical arrangement is:

Plant Sensors / F&G / ESD / DCS
↓
Plant Alert Controller / PLC
↓
Communication Network
↓
Field Alert Devices
↓
Personnel

Field devices can include:

  • Audible sounders

  • Electronic sirens

  • Horns

  • Strobe lights

  • Beacon lights

  • Combination sounder/beacons

  • Message displays

  • Mimic panels

  • Remote annunciator panels

  • PA/GA speakers

Typical Alarm Levels

A plant may configure different alarm levels depending on the project philosophy:

Level Example Typical Indication
Advisory Equipment abnormality Visual indication
Warning High gas concentration Sounder + beacon
High Alarm Significant hazardous condition Audible + visual alarm
Emergency Major gas/fire event Plant-wide alarm / PAGA
Evacuation Immediate danger Evacuation tone + voice message

The exact alarm levels and colors should be defined by the project Alarm Philosophy and Cause & Effect.

Plant Alert System vs PAGA

These systems can overlap, but they are not necessarily the same.

Feature Plant Alert System PAGA
Audible alarm ✓ ✓
Visual beacon/strobe ✓ ✓/interface
Voice announcements Optional Main function
Emergency evacuation ✓ ✓
Fire & Gas interface ✓ ✓
Zone-based alarms ✓ ✓
Alarm annunciation ✓ ✓
Public address Optional Yes
Two-way communication Usually no Optional
Speaker-line supervision Depending on system Usually important
Plant-wide emergency communication ✓ Yes

In simple terms: a Plant Alert System focuses on alerting personnel to plant conditions, while PAGA combines public-address communication with general/emergency alarms.

Typical Equipment

For an industrial Plant Alert System, the BOQ may include:

  1. Plant Alert Controller / PLC

  2. Alarm Management Software

  3. Remote I/O Panels

  4. Audible Sounders

  5. Electronic Sirens

  6. Visual Beacons

  7. Strobe Lights

  8. Combined Sounder/Beacon

  9. Alarm Annunciator Panels

  10. Remote Alarm Stations

  11. Industrial Ethernet Switches

  12. Fiber Optic Network

  13. UPS / 24 VDC Power Supply

  14. Interface Modules

  15. Junction Boxes

  16. Cables and Cable Glands

  17. Hazardous-area certified devices, where required.

Example of Operation

For example, if a gas detector detects a dangerous gas concentration:

Gas Detector → F&G System → Plant Alert System

The Plant Alert System may then:

  • Activate a red flashing beacon in the affected area.

  • Activate an audible alarm/sounder.

  • Display "GAS ALARM – AREA 3" on an annunciator.

  • Send the alarm to the control room.

  • Initiate an appropriate PAGA emergency message.

  • Provide alarm information to the operator.

  • Activate additional plant responses according to the approved Cause & Effect.

Hazardous Area Requirements

If Plant Alert devices are installed in classified hazardous areas, the equipment must have the appropriate certification based on the project hazardous-area classification, such as:

  • ATEX

  • IECEx

  • Class I, Division 1/2, where applicable

The selected equipment should also have suitable IP/NEMA environmental protection, temperature rating, corrosion resistance, and required ingress protection.

Recommended Technical Description

For a technical proposal, you can use:

The Plant Alert System shall provide a reliable and centralized means of notifying plant personnel of abnormal, hazardous and emergency conditions. The system shall receive alarm inputs from the Fire & Gas System, Emergency Shutdown System, DCS/SCADA and other approved plant systems and shall generate appropriate audible and visual alerts in the designated plant areas. The system shall support area-specific and plant-wide alarm functions, alarm prioritization, event monitoring and system diagnostics. Field notification devices shall include audible sounders, electronic sirens, visual beacons, strobes and combination audible/visual alarm devices as applicable. Equipment installed in hazardous areas shall be suitably certified in accordance with the applicable hazardous-area classification. The system shall be designed for high availability and shall be integrated with the plant emergency communication and safety systems in accordance with the approved project specifications, Cause & Effect and Alarm Philosophy.

heading: IPPS System in a Plant
content:
In-Plant Paging System for a Gas Plant

An In-Plant Paging System is an industrial communication system used to provide voice announcements and paging between the control room, operating areas, process units, workshops, buildings, and field personnel within a gas plant.

It is primarily intended for routine operational communication, while emergency announcements and evacuation alarms are normally handled through the PAGA (Public Address and General Alarm) system or an integrated PA/GA platform.

1. Purpose

The In-Plant Paging System allows operators and plant personnel to:

  • Make live voice announcements to selected areas or the entire plant.

  • Call individual areas or paging zones.

  • Communicate operational instructions.

  • Announce maintenance activities.

  • Notify personnel about equipment or process conditions.

  • Broadcast routine messages to field personnel.

  • Provide communication between control rooms and operating areas.

2. Typical Architecture

A typical IP-based system can be arranged as:

Control Room / Operator Console
↓
Paging Server / IP-PBX / Paging Controller
↓
Industrial Ethernet Network
↓
Network Amplifier / Zone Controller
↓
Speaker Lines
↓
Field Speakers

For a gas plant, the system can be divided into multiple paging zones, such as:

  • Process Area

  • Compressor Area

  • Utility Area

  • Tank Farm

  • Loading/Unloading Area

  • Control Room

  • Workshop

  • Warehouse

  • Administration Building

  • Substation

  • Maintenance Area

3. Main Equipment

Equipment Function
Paging Server/Controller Central system control
Operator Paging Console Allows operators to select zones and make announcements
Microphone Station Live voice paging
IP Paging Station Network-based paging
Network Amplifier Converts and amplifies IP audio
Power Amplifier Provides required speaker power
Horn/Trumpet Speaker Outdoor/process-area coverage
Wall/Ceiling Speaker Indoor areas
Explosion-Proof Speaker Hazardous areas
Speaker Junction Box Speaker-line termination
Network Switch IP communication
UPS Backup power
Monitoring System Fault and equipment monitoring

4. Hazardous Area Application

Gas plants contain classified hazardous areas. Therefore, speakers and paging stations installed in hazardous locations must have suitable certification according to the project hazardous-area classification.

Typical field devices may include:

  • ATEX/IECEx-certified horn speakers

  • Explosion-proof paging stations

  • Weatherproof speakers

  • Hazardous-area junction boxes

  • Certified cable glands and accessories

For example, a process area classified as Zone 1 may require a suitable IECEx/ATEX Zone 1 speaker, while equipment in a non-hazardous control room can use standard indoor IP speakers.

5. Zone Paging

One of the important features is selective zone paging.

For example, an operator can select:

Zone 1 – Compressor Area

and make an announcement only in that area.

Alternatively:

All Zones → Plant-wide announcement

This prevents unnecessary announcements from disturbing personnel in unaffected areas.

6. Integration with PAGA

In a gas plant, the In-Plant Paging System is often integrated with or incorporated into the PAGA system.

Function In-Plant Paging PAGA
Routine announcements Yes Yes
Zone paging Yes Yes
Plant-wide paging Yes Yes
Emergency alarm Usually interface Yes
Evacuation message Usually interface Yes
Fire & Gas interface Interface Yes
Emergency priority Limited/controlled High priority
Hazardous-area speakers Yes Yes
Speaker supervision Depending on system Normally required

The important principle is that emergency messages should have priority over routine paging.

For example:

Routine paging → Emergency alarm → Evacuation message

The emergency announcement interrupts normal paging according to the approved priority and cause-and-effect philosophy.

7. Example of Operation

An operator in the control room needs to inform technicians working near a compressor.

The operator selects:

Compressor Area → Paging Microphone → Announcement

The message is transmitted through the IP network to the designated amplifier and speaker zone.

Operator Console → IP Network → Amplifier → Compressor Area Speakers

Personnel in other plant areas do not hear the announcement unless the operator selects those zones.

8. Recommended Technical Proposal Description

You can use the following wording in your gas plant technical proposal:

The In-Plant Paging System shall provide a reliable and flexible voice communication facility for operational and routine paging throughout the gas plant. The system shall enable authorized operators to make live announcements to individual paging zones, selected groups of zones, or the complete plant as required. The system shall comprise paging consoles/stations, central controller or server, network infrastructure, amplifiers, speaker-line distribution and suitable field loudspeakers. The system shall support zone-based paging, priority management, system monitoring and fault indication. Equipment installed within classified hazardous areas shall be suitably certified in accordance with the applicable hazardous-area classification and project requirements. The In-Plant Paging System shall be integrated with the PAGA/General Alarm System where required, with emergency alarms and messages assigned higher priority than routine paging. The complete system shall be designed for reliable operation, high availability, ease of maintenance and future expansion.

9. Typical System for a Gas Plant

A practical solution could therefore consist of:

Central Control Room

  • Paging Server/Controller

  • Operator Paging Console

  • Microphone Station

  • System Management Workstation

Communication Network

  • Core/Distribution Switches

  • Fiber Optic Backbone

  • Industrial Ethernet Switches

Field

  • Network Amplifiers

  • 100 V speaker lines

  • Explosion-proof/IECEx/ATEX speakers

  • Weatherproof horn speakers

  • Paging stations

Integration

  • PAGA

  • Fire & Gas System

  • DCS

  • ESD

  • Plant Alert System

For the type of gas-plant PAGA/paging BOQ you've been working on, the In-Plant Paging System can be specified as a separate routine paging function or as part of an integrated PAGA system, depending on the client's SOW and Cause & Effect requirements.

heading: Process CCTV
content:
Process CCTV is a specialized industrial video surveillance system used to monitor, observe, and control critical process operations in facilities such as oil & gas plants, refineries, petrochemical plants, power plants, and chemical plants.

Unlike normal security CCTV, which mainly monitors people, buildings, and perimeter areas, Process CCTV focuses on the plant process and equipment

Typical Process CCTV Applications

Process CCTV can be used to monitor:

  • Flare stacks and flare tips

  • Furnaces and heaters

  • Boilers

  • Burners and pilot flames

  • Gas turbines

  • Compressors

  • Pumps

  • Storage tanks

  • Loading/unloading areas

  • Process vessels

  • Conveyor systems

  • Valve stations

  • Pipe racks

  • Critical machinery

  • Remote/unmanned process areas

Process CCTV vs Security CCTV

Feature Process CCTV Security CCTV
Main purpose Monitor plant/process operation Security & surveillance
Main target Equipment/process People, vehicles, perimeter
Typical location Process units Buildings, gates, perimeter
Camera type Fixed, PTZ, thermal, explosion-proof Dome, bullet, PTZ
Thermal camera Frequently used Optional
Flame monitoring Common Normally not required
Integration DCS, SCADA, F&G, VMS VMS, ACS, security systems
Analytics Process/equipment monitoring Intrusion/person/vehicle analytics
Hazardous area Often required Depending on location

Example: Furnace Monitoring

For a refinery furnace, Process CCTV may use an explosion-proof camera or specialized thermal camera to monitor the furnace from a safe location.

The operator can observe:

Camera → Furnace/Burner → Video transmission → VMS → Control Room Monitor

If integrated with plant systems, an abnormal condition can also generate an alarm or event for the operator.

Key Difference

A simple way to remember it:

Security CCTV asks: "Who is entering the plant?"
Process CCTV asks: "What is happening in the plant process?"

For an oil & gas project, Process CCTV is often integrated with the VMS/CCTV system, DCS/SCADA, F&G and control-room video wall, depending on the project requirements.
